Politics
Politics is the activity of settling affairs in an organized <color=#3366CC>society</color>. Politics is usually concerned with resolving issues within
a society via a <color=#3366CC>government</color>. Politicians are individuals engaged in the activity of politics. The branch of <color=#3366CC>social science</color>
that studies politics and government is referred to as <color=#3366CC>political science</color>.
A variety of methods are deployed in politics, which include <color=#3366CC>promoting one's own political views</color> among people,
<color=#3366CC>negotiation</color> with other political subjects, making <color=#3366CC>laws</color>, and exercising internal and external force, including <color=#3366CC>warfare</color>
against adversaries. Politics is exercised on a wide range of social levels, from <color=#3366CC>clans</color> and <color=#3366CC>tribes</color> of traditional <color=#3366CC>societies</color>,

through modern <color=#3366CC>local governments</color>, <color=#3366CC>companies</color> and <color=#3366CC>institutions</color> up to <color=#3366CC>sovereign states</color>, to the <color=#3366CC>international level</color>.
In modern <color=#3366CC>states</color>, people often form <color=#3366CC>political parties</color> to represent their ideas. Members of a party often agree to take the
same position on many issues and agree to support the same changes to law and the same leaders. An <color=#3366CC>election</color> is
usually a competition between different parties.
A <color=#3366CC>political system</color> is a framework which defines acceptable political methods within a society. The <color=#3366CC>history of political</color>

<color=#3366CC>thought</color> can be traced back to early antiquity, with seminal works such as <color=#3366CC>Plato</color>'s <color=#3366CC>Republic</color>, <color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color>'s <color=#3366CC>Politics</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Confucius</color>'s political manuscripts and <color=#3366CC>Chanakya</color>'s <color=#3366CC>Arthashastra</color>.
Politics may be used positively in the context of a "political solution" which is compromising and non-violent, or
descriptively as "the art or science of government", but the word often also carries a negative connotation.
Etymology
The English word politics has its roots in the Greek word polis (or poleis) which means "city". <color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color>'s classic work,
<color=#3366CC>Politiká</color> used the <color=#3366CC>Ancient Greek</color> term politiká. In the mid-15th century, Aristotle's composition was rendered in <color=#3366CC>Early</color>
<color=#3366CC>Modern English</color> as Polettiques, which became Politics in <color=#3366CC>Modern English</color>.
The singular politic first attested in English in 1430, coming from <color=#3366CC>Middle French</color> politique—itself derived from politicus, a
Latinization of the Greek (politikos) from (polites) and (polis).
Approaches
Extensive and limited
Adrian Leftwich has differentiated views of politics based on how extensive or limited their perception of what accounts
as 'political' is. The extensive view sees politics as present across the sphere of human social relations, while the
limited view restricts it to certain contexts. For example, in a more restrictive way, politics may be viewed as primarily
about <color=#3366CC>governance</color>, while a feminist perspective could argue that sites which have been viewed traditionally as
non-political, should indeed be viewed as political as well. This latter position is encapsulated in the slogan "the
personal is political", which disputes the distinction between private and public issues. Politics may also be defined by
the use of power, as has been argued by Robert A. Dahl.
Moralism and realism
Some perspectives on politics view it empirically as an exercise of power, while others see it as a social function with a
normative basis. This distinction has sometimes been called the difference between political moralism and political
realism. For moralists, politics is closely linked to <color=#3366CC>ethics</color>, and is at its extreme in <color=#3366CC>utopian</color> thinking. For example,
according to <color=#3366CC>Hannah Arendt</color>, the view of <color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color> was that, "to be political…meant that everything was decided through
words and persuasion and not through violence"; while according to Bernard Crick, "politics is the way in which free
societies are governed. Politics is politics, and other forms of rule are something else." In contrast, for realists, who
some include figures such as <color=#3366CC>Niccolò Machiavelli</color>, <color=#3366CC>Thomas Hobbes</color>, and Harold Lasswell, the true nature of politics
reflects human desire for rule and the aggrandizement of self interests rather than moralism.
Conflict and co-operation
Agonism argues that politics essentially comes down to conflict between conflicting interests. Political scientist Elmer
Schattschneider argued that "at the root of all politics is the universal language of conflict", while for <color=#3366CC>Carl Schmitt</color> the
essence of politics is the distinction of 'friend' from 'foe'. This is in direct contrast to the more co-operative views of
politics by Aristotle and Crick. However, a more mixed view between these extremes is provided by Irish political
scientist Michael Laver, who noted that:Politics is about the characteristic blend of conflict and co-operation that can be
found so often in human interactions. Pure conflict is war. Pure co-operation is true love. Politics is a mixture of both.
History
Prehistoric
Early human forms of social organization—bands and tribes—lacked centralized political structures. These are
sometimes referred to as <color=#3366CC>stateless societies</color>.
Early states
In ancient history, <color=#3366CC>civilizations</color> did not have definite boundaries as <color=#3366CC>states</color> have today, and their borders could be more
accurately described as frontiers. <color=#3366CC>Early dynastic Sumer</color>, and <color=#3366CC>early dynastic Egypt</color> were the <color=#3366CC>first civilizations</color> to define
their <color=#3366CC>borders</color>. Moreover, up to the 12th century, many people lived in non-state societies. These range from relatively
egalitarian bands and <color=#3366CC>tribes</color> to complex and highly stratified <color=#3366CC>chiefdoms</color>.
State formation
There are a number of different theories and hypotheses regarding early state formation that seek generalizations to
explain why <color=#3366CC>the state</color> developed in some places but not others. Other scholars believe that generalizations are
unhelpful and that each case of early state formation should be treated on its own.
Voluntary theories contend that diverse groups of people came together to form states as a result of some shared
rational interest. The theories largely focus on the development of agriculture, and the population and organizational
pressure that followed and resulted in state formation. One of the most prominent theories of early and primary state
formation is the hydraulic hypothesis, which contends that the state was a result of the need to build and maintain
large-scale irrigation projects.
<color=#3366CC>Conflict theories</color> of state formation regard conflict and dominance of some population over another population as key to
the formation of states. In contrast with voluntary theories, these arguments believe that people do not voluntarily agree
to create a state to maximize benefits, but that states form due to some form of oppression by one group over others.
Some theories in turn argue that warfare was critical for state formation.
Ancient history
The first states of sorts were those of <color=#3366CC>early dynastic Sumer</color> and <color=#3366CC>early dynastic Egypt</color>, which arose from the <color=#3366CC>Uruk period</color>
and <color=#3366CC>Predynastic Egypt</color> respectively around approximately 3000 BC. Early dynastic Egypt was based around the <color=#3366CC>Nile</color>
<color=#3366CC>River</color> in the north-east of <color=#3366CC>Africa</color>, the kingdom's boundaries being based around the Nile and stretching to areas where

<color=#3366CC>oases</color> existed. Early dynastic <color=#3366CC>Sumer</color> was located in southern <color=#3366CC>Mesopotamia</color>, with its borders extending from the <color=#3366CC>Persian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Gulf</color> to parts of the <color=#3366CC>Euphrates</color> and <color=#3366CC>Tigris</color> rivers.
Egyptians, Romans, and the Greeks were the first people known to have explicitly formulated a political philosophy of
the state, and to have rationally analyzed political institutions. Prior to this, states were described and justified in terms
of religious myths.
Several important political innovations of <color=#3366CC>classical antiquity</color> came from the Greek city-states (polis) and the <color=#3366CC>Roman</color>
<color=#3366CC>Republic</color>. The Greek city-states before the 4th century granted <color=#3366CC>citizenship</color> rights to their free population; in <color=#3366CC>Athens</color>
these rights <color=#3366CC>were combined</color> with a <color=#3366CC>directly democratic</color> form of government that was to have a long afterlife in political
thought and history.
Modern states
The <color=#3366CC>Peace of Westphalia</color> (1648) is considered by <color=#3366CC>political scientists</color> to be the beginning of the modern international
system, in which external powers should avoid interfering in another country's domestic affairs. The principle of
non-interference in other countries' domestic affairs was laid out in the mid-18th century by Swiss jurist Emer de Vattel.
States became the primary institutional agents in an interstate system of relations. The Peace of Westphalia is said to
have ended attempts to impose supranational authority on European states. The "Westphalian" doctrine of states as
independent agents was bolstered by the rise in 19th century thought of <color=#3366CC>nationalism</color>, under which legitimate <color=#3366CC>states</color>
were assumed to correspond to <color=#3366CC>nations</color>—groups of people united by language and culture.
In <color=#3366CC>Europe</color>, during the 18th century, the classic non-national states were the multinational <color=#3366CC>empires</color>: the <color=#3366CC>Austrian Empire</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Kingdom of France</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Hungary</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Russian Empire</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Spanish Empire</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman Empire</color>, and the
<color=#3366CC>British Empire</color>. Such empires also existed in Asia, Africa, and the Americas; in the <color=#3366CC>Muslim world</color>, immediately after the
<color=#3366CC>death of Muhammad</color> in 632, <color=#3366CC>Caliphates</color> were established, which developed into multi-ethnic transnational empires. The
multinational empire was an <color=#3366CC>absolute monarchy</color> ruled by a king, <color=#3366CC>emperor</color> or <color=#3366CC>sultan</color>. The population belonged to many
ethnic groups, and they spoke many languages. The empire was dominated by one ethnic group, and their language
was usually the language of public administration. The ruling <color=#3366CC>dynasty</color> was usually, but not always, from that group.
Some of the smaller European states were not so ethnically diverse, but were also dynastic states, ruled by a royal
house. A few of the smaller states survived, such as the independent principalities of <color=#3366CC>Liechtenstein</color>, <color=#3366CC>Andorra</color>, <color=#3366CC>Monaco</color>,
and the republic of <color=#3366CC>San Marino</color>.
Most theories see the nation state as a 19th-century European phenomenon, facilitated by developments such as
state-mandated education, mass <color=#3366CC>literacy</color>, and <color=#3366CC>mass media</color>. However, historians also note the early emergence of a
relatively unified state and identity in <color=#3366CC>Portugal</color> and the Dutch Republic. Scholars such as Steven Weber, David
Woodward, <color=#3366CC>Michel Foucault</color>, and Jeremy Black have advanced the hypothesis that the nation state did not arise out of
political ingenuity or an unknown undetermined source, nor was it an accident of history or political invention. Rather,
the nation state is an inadvertent byproduct of 15th-century intellectual discoveries in <color=#3366CC>political economy</color>, <color=#3366CC>capitalism</color>,

<color=#3366CC>mercantilism</color>, <color=#3366CC>political geography</color>, and <color=#3366CC>geography</color> combined with <color=#3366CC>cartography</color> and <color=#3366CC>advances in map-making</color>
<color=#3366CC>technologies</color>.
Some nation states, such as <color=#3366CC>Germany</color> and <color=#3366CC>Italy</color>, came into existence at least partly as a result of political campaigns by
<color=#3366CC>nationalists</color>, during the 19th century. In both cases, the territory was previously divided among other states, some of
them very small. Liberal ideas of <color=#3366CC>free trade</color> played a role in German unification, which was preceded by a customs
union, the Zollverein. National <color=#3366CC>self-determination</color> was a key aspect of United States President <color=#3366CC>Woodrow Wilson</color>'s

<color=#3366CC>Fourteen Points</color>, leading to the dissolution of the <color=#3366CC>Austro-Hungarian Empire</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman Empire</color> after the <color=#3366CC>First</color>

<color=#3366CC>World War</color>, while the <color=#3366CC>Russian Empire</color> became the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color> after the <color=#3366CC>Russian Civil War</color>. <color=#3366CC>Decolonization</color> lead to the
creation of new nation states in place of multinational empires in the <color=#3366CC>Third World</color>.
Globalization
Political globalization began in the 20th century through <color=#3366CC>intergovernmental organizations</color> and supranational unions. The

<color=#3366CC>League of Nations</color> was founded after <color=#3366CC>World War I</color>, and after <color=#3366CC>World War II</color> it was replaced by the <color=#3366CC>United Nations</color>.
Various <color=#3366CC>international treaties</color> have been signed through it. Regional integration has been pursued by political and fiscal

unions such as <color=#3366CC>BRICS</color>, the <color=#3366CC>African Union</color>, <color=#3366CC>ASEAN</color>, the <color=#3366CC>European Union</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Mercosur</color>. International political
institutions on the international level include the <color=#3366CC>International Criminal Court</color>, the <color=#3366CC>International Monetary Fund</color>, and the
<color=#3366CC>World Trade Organization</color>.
Political science
The study of politics is called political science. It comprises numerous subfields, namely three: <color=#3366CC>Comparative politics</color>,
<color=#3366CC>international relations</color> and <color=#3366CC>political philosophy</color>. Political science is related to, and draws upon, the fields of <color=#3366CC>economics</color>,

<color=#3366CC>law</color>, sociology, <color=#3366CC>history</color>, <color=#3366CC>philosophy</color>, <color=#3366CC>geography</color>, <color=#3366CC>psychology</color>, <color=#3366CC>psychiatry</color>, <color=#3366CC>anthropology</color>, and neurosciences.
<color=#3366CC>Comparative politics</color> is the science of comparison and teaching of different types of <color=#3366CC>constitutions</color>, political actors,
legislature and associated fields. <color=#3366CC>International relations</color> deals with the interaction between <color=#3366CC>nation-states</color> as well as
intergovernmental and transnational organizations. <color=#3366CC>Political philosophy</color> is more concerned with the nature of politics
and seeks knowledge about topics related to justice, legitimacy, liberty, and the legal foundations of ancient and
modern civilizations.
Political system
The political system defines the process for making official <color=#3366CC>government</color> decisions. It is usually compared to the legal
system, <color=#3366CC>economic system</color>, cultural system, and other social systems. According to David Easton, "A political system
can be designated as the interactions through which values are authoritatively allocated for a society." Each political
system is embedded in a society with its own political culture, and they in turn shape their societies through <color=#3366CC>public</color>
<color=#3366CC>policy</color>. The interactions between different political systems are the basis for global politics.
Forms of government
Forms of government can be classified by several ways. Generally, most governments are either <color=#3366CC>monarchies</color> (including

<color=#3366CC>constitutional monarchies</color>) and <color=#3366CC>republics</color> (usually <color=#3366CC>presidential</color>, <color=#3366CC>semi-presidential</color>, or <color=#3366CC>parliamentary</color>). Republics are the
most common form of government, with fewer nations being monarchies.
Another model of classifying regimes is by who runs them, such as in a <color=#3366CC>democracy</color> (rule of many), <color=#3366CC>oligarchy</color> (rule by
few), or <color=#3366CC>autocracy</color> (rule by one).
Source of authority
Vertical integration
In terms of level of vertical integration, political systems can be divided into (from least to most integrated)
<color=#3366CC>confederations</color>, <color=#3366CC>federations</color>, and <color=#3366CC>unitary states</color>.
State
All the above forms of government are variations of the same basic polity, the <color=#3366CC>sovereign state</color>. The <color=#3366CC>state</color> has been
defined by <color=#3366CC>Max Weber</color> as a political entity that has monopoly on violence within its territory, while the Montevideo
Convention holds that states need to have a defined territory; a permanent population; a government; and a capacity to
enter into international relations.
A stateless society is a <color=#3366CC>society</color> that is not <color=#3366CC>governed</color> by a <color=#3366CC>state</color>. In stateless societies, there is little concentration of
authority; most positions of authority that do exist are very limited in <color=#3366CC>power</color> and are generally not permanently held
positions; and social bodies that resolve disputes through predefined rules tend to be small. Stateless societies are
highly variable in economic organization and cultural practices.
While stateless societies were the norm in human prehistory, few stateless societies exist today; almost the entire
global population resides within the jurisdiction of a <color=#3366CC>sovereign state</color>. In some regions, nominal state authorities may be
very weak and wield <color=#3366CC>little or no actual power</color>. Over the course of history most stateless peoples have been <color=#3366CC>integrated</color>
<color=#3366CC>into the state-based societies around them</color>.
Some political ideologies consider the state undesirable, and thus consider the formation of a stateless society a goal
to be achieved. A central tenet of <color=#3366CC>anarchism</color> is the advocacy of society without states. The type of society sought for
varies significantly between <color=#3366CC>anarchist schools of thought</color>, ranging from extreme <color=#3366CC>individualism</color> to complete <color=#3366CC>collectivism</color>.
In <color=#3366CC>Marxism</color>, Marx's theory of the state considers that in a post-capitalist society the state, an undesirable institution,
would be unnecessary and wither away. A related concept is that of <color=#3366CC>stateless communism</color>, a phrase sometimes used
to describe Marx's anticipated post-capitalist society.
Constitutions
<color=#3366CC>Constitutions</color> are written documents that specify and limit the powers of the different branches of government. Although
a constitution is a written document, there is also an unwritten constitution. The unwritten constitution is continually
being written by the legislative and judiciary branch of government; this is just one of those cases in which the nature of
the circumstances determines the form of government that is most appropriate. England did set the fashion of written
constitutions during the <color=#3366CC>Civil War</color> but after the <color=#3366CC>Restoration</color> abandoned them to be taken up later by the <color=#3366CC>American</color>

<color=#3366CC>Colonies</color> after their <color=#3366CC>emancipation</color> and then <color=#3366CC>France</color> after the <color=#3366CC>Revolution</color> and the rest of Europe including the European
colonies.
Political culture
Political culture describes how <color=#3366CC>culture</color> impacts politics. Every <color=#3366CC>political system</color> is embedded in a particular political
culture. Lucian Pye's definition is that, "Political culture is the set of attitudes, beliefs, and sentiments, which give order
and meaning to a political process and which provide the underlying assumptions and rules that govern behavior in the
political system."
<color=#3366CC>Trust</color> is a major factor in political culture, as its level determines the capacity of the state to function. Postmaterialism is
the degree to which a political culture is concerned with issues which are not of immediate physical or material concern,
such as <color=#3366CC>human rights</color> and <color=#3366CC>environmentalism</color>. <color=#3366CC>Religion</color> has also an impact on political culture.
Political dysfunction
Political dysfunctions include gridlock and voter suppression.
Political corruption
Proxy politics
The term "proxy politics" refers to specific forms of political influences and actions that are conducted through <color=#3366CC>proxy</color>
<color=#3366CC>political parties</color> (mainly in <color=#3366CC>domestic politics</color>), or through <color=#3366CC>proxy wars</color> (mainly in <color=#3366CC>international politics</color>).
Insincere politics
The words "politics" and "political" are sometimes used as pejoratives to mean political action that is deemed to be
overzealous, performative, or insincere.
Levels of politics
Macropolitics
Macropolitics can either describe political issues that affect an entire political system (e.g. the <color=#3366CC>nation state</color>), or refer to
interactions between political systems (e.g. <color=#3366CC>international relations</color>).
Global politics (or world politics) covers all aspects of politics that affect multiple political systems, in practice meaning
any political phenomenon crossing national borders. This can include <color=#3366CC>cities</color>, nation-states, <color=#3366CC>multinational corporations</color>,
<color=#3366CC>non-governmental organizations</color> or <color=#3366CC>international organizations</color>. An important element is international relations: the
relations between nation-states may be peaceful when they are conducted through <color=#3366CC>diplomacy</color>, or they may be violent,
which is described as <color=#3366CC>war</color>. States that are able to exert strong international influence are referred to as <color=#3366CC>superpowers</color>,
whereas less-powerful ones may be called <color=#3366CC>regional</color> or middle powers. The international system of power is called the
world order, which is affected by the <color=#3366CC>balance of power</color> that defines the degree of polarity in the system. Emerging
powers are potentially destabilizing to it, especially if they display revanchism or irredentism.
Politics inside the limits of political systems, which in contemporary context correspond to national <color=#3366CC>borders</color>, are referred

to as <color=#3366CC>domestic politics</color>. This includes most forms of <color=#3366CC>public policy</color>, such as <color=#3366CC>social policy</color>, <color=#3366CC>economic policy</color>, or <color=#3366CC>law</color>
<color=#3366CC>enforcement</color>, which are executed by the state <color=#3366CC>bureaucracy</color>.
Mesopolitics
Mesopolitics describes the politics of intermediary structures within a political system, such as <color=#3366CC>national political parties</color>
or movements.
A political party is a political organization that typically seeks to attain and maintain political power within <color=#3366CC>government</color>,
usually by participating in <color=#3366CC>political campaigns</color>, educational outreach, or <color=#3366CC>protest actions</color>. Parties often espouse an
expressed <color=#3366CC>ideology</color> or vision, bolstered by a written platform with specific goals, forming a coalition among disparate
interests.
Political parties within a particular political system together form the party system, which can be either multiparty,
two-party, dominant-party, or <color=#3366CC>one-party</color>, depending on the level of pluralism. This is affected by characteristics of the
political system, including its <color=#3366CC>electoral system</color>. According to Duverger's law, first-past-the-post systems are likely to lead
to two-party systems, while proportional representation systems are more likely to create a multiparty system.
Micropolitics
Micropolitics describes the actions of individual actors within the political system. This is often described as political
participation.
Political values
Democracy
Democracy is a system of processing conflicts in which outcomes depend on what participants do, but no single force
controls what occurs and its outcomes. The uncertainty of outcomes is inherent in democracy. Democracy makes all
forces struggle repeatedly to realize their interests and devolves power from groups of people to sets of rules.
Among modern political theorists, there are three contending conceptions of democracy: aggregative, deliberative, and
radical.
Aggregation
The theory of aggregative democracy claims that the aim of the democratic processes is to solicit the preferences of
citizens, and aggregate them together to determine what social policies the society should adopt. Therefore,
proponents of this view hold that democratic participation should primarily focus on <color=#3366CC>voting</color>, where the policy with the
most votes gets implemented.
Different variants of aggregative democracy exist. Under minimalism, democracy is a system of government in which
citizens have given teams of political leaders the right to rule in periodic elections. According to this minimalist
conception, citizens cannot and should not "rule" because, for example, on most issues, most of the time, they have no
clear views or their views are not well-founded. <color=#3366CC>Joseph Schumpeter</color> articulated this view most famously in his book
<color=#3366CC>Capitalism, Socialism, and Democracy</color>. Contemporary proponents of minimalism include William H. Riker, Adam
Przeworski, and <color=#3366CC>Richard Posner</color>.
According to the theory of <color=#3366CC>direct democracy</color>, on the other hand, citizens should vote directly, not through their
representatives, on legislative proposals. Proponents of direct democracy offer varied reasons to support this view.
Political activity can be valuable in itself, it socialises and educates citizens, and popular participation can check
powerful elites. Most importantly, citizens do not rule themselves unless they directly decide laws and policies.
Governments will tend to produce laws and policies that are close to the views of the median voter—with half to their
left and the other half to their right. This is not a desirable outcome as it represents the action of self-interested and
somewhat unaccountable political elites competing for votes. Anthony Downs suggests that ideological political parties
are necessary to act as a mediating broker between individual and governments. Downs laid out this view in his 1957
book An Economic Theory of Democracy.
Polyarchy
Robert A. Dahl argues that the fundamental democratic principle is that, when it comes to binding collective decisions,
each person in a political community is entitled to have his/her interests be given equal consideration (not necessarily
that all people are equally satisfied by the collective decision). He uses the term polyarchy to refer to societies in which
there exists a certain set of institutions and procedures which are perceived as leading to such democracy. First and
foremost among these institutions is the regular occurrence of free and open <color=#3366CC>elections</color> which are used to select
representatives who then manage all or most of the public policy of the society. However, these polyarchic procedures
may not create a full democracy if, for example, poverty prevents political participation. Similarly, <color=#3366CC>Ronald Dworkin</color>
argues that "democracy is a substantive, not a merely procedural, ideal".
Deliberation
Deliberative democracy is based on the notion that democracy is government by deliberation. Unlike aggregative
democracy, deliberative democracy holds that, for a democratic decision to be legitimate, it must be preceded by
authentic deliberation, not merely the aggregation of preferences that occurs in voting. Authentic deliberation is
deliberation among decision-makers that is free from distortions of unequal political power, such as power a
decision-maker obtained through economic wealth or the support of interest groups. If the decision-makers cannot
reach consensus after authentically deliberating on a proposal, then they vote on the proposal using a form of majority
rule.
Equality
Equality is a state of affairs in which all people within a specific <color=#3366CC>society</color> or isolated group have the same <color=#3366CC>social status</color>,

especially <color=#3366CC>socioeconomic status</color>, including protection of <color=#3366CC>human rights</color> and <color=#3366CC>dignity</color>, as well as access to certain <color=#3366CC>social</color>
<color=#3366CC>goods</color> and social services. Furthermore, it may also include health equality, <color=#3366CC>economic equality</color> and other <color=#3366CC>social</color>

<color=#3366CC>securities</color>. <color=#3366CC>Social equality</color> requires the absence of legally enforced <color=#3366CC>social class</color> or <color=#3366CC>caste</color> boundaries and the absence of
<color=#3366CC>discrimination</color> based on by an inalienable aspect of a person's identity. To this end, there must be equal justice under
law, and equal opportunity regardless of, sex, gender, ethnicity, age, sexual orientation, origin, caste or class, income
or property, language, <color=#3366CC>religion</color>, convictions, opinions, health or disability.
Political spectrum
A common way of understanding politics is through the left–right political spectrum, which ranges from <color=#3366CC>left-wing politics</color>
via <color=#3366CC>centrism</color> to <color=#3366CC>right-wing politics</color>. This classification is comparatively recent and dates from the <color=#3366CC>French Revolution</color>,
when those members of the National Assembly who supported the <color=#3366CC>republic</color>, the common people and a <color=#3366CC>secular society</color>
sat on the left and supporters of the <color=#3366CC>monarchy</color>, aristocratic privilege and the Church sat on the right.
Today, the left is generally <color=#3366CC>progressivist</color>, seeking social <color=#3366CC>progress</color> in <color=#3366CC>society</color>. The more extreme elements of the left,
named the <color=#3366CC>far-left</color>, tend to support <color=#3366CC>revolutionary</color> means for achieving this. This includes ideologies such as
<color=#3366CC>Communism</color> and <color=#3366CC>Marxism</color>. The <color=#3366CC>center-left</color>, on the other hand, advocates for more reformist approaches, for example
that of <color=#3366CC>social democracy</color>.
In contrast, the right is generally motivated by <color=#3366CC>conservatism</color>, which seeks to conserve what it sees as the important
elements of society such as law and order, limited government and preserving individual freedoms. The <color=#3366CC>far-right</color> goes
beyond this, and often represents a <color=#3366CC>reactionary</color> turn against progress, seeking to undo it. Examples of such ideologies
have included <color=#3366CC>Fascism</color> and <color=#3366CC>Nazism</color>. The <color=#3366CC>center-right</color> may be less clear-cut and more mixed in this regard, with
<color=#3366CC>neoconservatives</color> supporting the spread of <color=#3366CC>free markets</color> and <color=#3366CC>capitalism</color>, and one-nation conservatives more open to
social welfare programs.
According to Norberto Bobbio, one of the major exponents of this distinction, the left believes in attempting to eradicate
social inequality—believing it to be unethical or unnatural, while the right regards most social inequality as the result of
ineradicable natural inequalities, and sees attempts to enforce social equality as utopian or authoritarian. Some
ideologies, notably <color=#3366CC>Christian Democracy</color>, claim to combine left and right-wing politics; according to Geoffrey K. Roberts
and Patricia Hogwood, "In terms of ideology, Christian Democracy has incorporated many of the views held by liberals,
conservatives and socialists within a wider framework of moral and Christian principles." Movements which claim or
formerly claimed to be above the left-right divide include Fascist Terza Posizione economic politics in Italy and
Peronism in Argentina.
The salience of political issues can be measured with surveys and can vary over time.
Freedom
Political freedom (also known as political liberty or autonomy) is a central <color=#3366CC>concept</color> in political thought and one of the
most important features of <color=#3366CC>democratic</color> societies. Negative liberty has been described as freedom from oppression or
coercion and unreasonable external constraints on action, often enacted through <color=#3366CC>civil and political rights</color>, while positive
liberty is the absence of disabling conditions for an individual and the fulfillment of enabling conditions, e.g. economic
compulsion, in a society. This capability approach to freedom requires <color=#3366CC>economic, social and cultural rights</color> in order to
be realized.
Authoritarianism and libertarianism
<color=#3366CC>Authoritarianism</color> and libertarianism disagree the amount of individual <color=#3366CC>freedom</color> each person possesses in that society
relative to the state. One author describes authoritarian political systems as those where "individual <color=#3366CC>rights</color> and goals
are subjugated to group goals, expectations and conformities", while libertarians generally oppose the <color=#3366CC>state</color> and hold
the <color=#3366CC>individual</color> as sovereign. In their purest form, libertarians are <color=#3366CC>anarchists</color>, who argue for the total abolition of the state,
of <color=#3366CC>political parties</color> and of other political entities, while the purest authoritarians are, by definition, <color=#3366CC>totalitarians</color> who
support state control over all aspects of society.
For instance, <color=#3366CC>classical liberalism</color> (also known as <color=#3366CC>laissez-faire</color> liberalism) is a doctrine stressing individual freedom and

<color=#3366CC>limited government</color>. This includes the importance of human rationality, individual <color=#3366CC>property rights</color>, <color=#3366CC>free markets</color>, <color=#3366CC>natural</color>
<color=#3366CC>rights</color>, the protection of <color=#3366CC>civil liberties</color>, constitutional limitation of government, and individual freedom from restraint as

exemplified in the writings of <color=#3366CC>John Locke</color>, <color=#3366CC>Adam Smith</color>, <color=#3366CC>David Hume</color>, <color=#3366CC>David Ricardo</color>, <color=#3366CC>Voltaire</color>, <color=#3366CC>Montesquieu</color> and others.
According to the libertarian Institute for Humane Studies, "the libertarian, or 'classical liberal', perspective is that
individual well-being, prosperity, and social harmony are fostered by 'as much liberty as possible' and 'as little
government as necessary'." For anarchist political philosopher L. Susan Brown (1993), "liberalism and <color=#3366CC>anarchism</color> are
two political philosophies that are fundamentally concerned with individual <color=#3366CC>freedom</color> yet differ from one another in very
distinct ways. Anarchism shares with liberalism a radical commitment to individual freedom while rejecting liberalism's
competitive property relations."
Charles de Gaulle Airport
Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport, also known as Roissy Airport, is the primary international airport serving <color=#3366CC>Paris</color>, the
capital of <color=#3366CC>France</color>. The airport opened in 1974 and is located in Roissy-en-France, 23 km northeast of the city centre of
Paris. It is named after World War II leader and French president <color=#3366CC>Charles de Gaulle</color>, whose initials form its IATA airport
code. It is one of two airports to serve the greater Paris area, the other being Orly Airport.
Charles de Gaulle Airport serves as the principal <color=#3366CC>hub</color> for <color=#3366CC>Air France</color>, as well as an operating base for easyJet. It is
operated by Groupe ADP (Aéroports de Paris) under the brand Paris Aéroport.
In 2024, the airport handled 70,290,260 passengers and 466,543 aircraft movements, making it the world's fourteenth
busiest airport and Europe's third busiest airport (after <color=#3366CC>London–Heathrow</color> and Istanbul) in terms of passenger numbers.
Charles de Gaulle is the busiest airport within the <color=#3366CC>European Union</color>. In terms of cargo traffic, the airport is the second
busiest in Europe, after Frankfurt, handling 1,914,681 tonnes of cargo in 2024. As of 2025, it was the airport served by
the second highest number of <color=#3366CC>airlines</color>, after Suvarnabhumi Airport, with 105 airlines operating from it.
Régis Lacote has been the director of the airport since 14 November 2022.
Location
Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport covers 32.38 km2 of land. The airport area, including terminals and runways, spans
over three départements and six communes:
• Seine-et-Marne département: Le Mesnil-Amelot (Terminal 2E, Satellites S3 and S4, and Terminal 2F), Mauregard
(Terminals 1, 3), and Mitry-Mory (Terminal 2G) communes;
• Seine-Saint-Denis département: Tremblay-en-France (Terminals 2A, 2B, 2C, 2D and Roissypôle) commune;
• Val-d'Oise département: Roissy-en-France and Épiais-lès-Louvres communes.
The choice of constructing an international aviation hub outside of central Paris was made due to a limited prospect of
potential relocations or expropriations and the possibility of further expanding the airport in the future.
Management of the airport lies solely on the authority of Groupe ADP, which also manages Orly (south of Paris), Le
Bourget (to the immediate southwest of Charles de Gaulle Airport, now used for general aviation and Paris Air Shows),
several smaller airfields in the suburbs of Paris, and other airports directly or indirectly worldwide.

Corporate identity
On 14 April 2016, the Groupe ADP rolled out the Connect 2020 corporate strategy and the commercial brand Paris
Aéroport was applied to all Parisian airports, including Le Bourget airport.
Terminals
Charles de Gaulle Airport has three terminals: Terminal 1 is the oldest and situated opposite to Terminal 3; Terminal 2
is located at another side with 7 sub-terminal buildings (2A to 2G). Terminal 2 was originally built exclusively for <color=#3366CC>Air</color>
<color=#3366CC>France</color>; since then it has been expanded significantly and now houses other airlines. Terminals 2A to 2F are
interconnected by elevated walkways and situated next to each other. Terminal 2G is a satellite building connected by
shuttle bus.
Terminal 1
Terminal 1 closed in March 2020 in response to the drop in traffic during the COVID-19 pandemic. ADP used this time
for a €250 million refurbishment. Completed in 2023, the refurbishment included the creation of a new junction building
linking satellites 1, 2 and 3, and modernisation of the central body of the terminal. Various design details in the
refurbished terminal pay homage to the circular shape of the original Andreu design. The upgraded Terminal 1 also
features a new departure lounge designed by French designers Maxime Liautard and Hugo Toro, which reflects the
ambiance of a Parisian bistro.
The terminal is primarily used by Star Alliance airlines with a few exceptions. Other carriers include Oneworld carriers
Qatar Airways and SriLankan Airlines; SkyTeam carrier Saudia; and non-alliance carriers including Aer Lingus, Etihad
Airways, Eurowings, Icelandair, and Kuwait Airways.
Terminal 2
Terminal 2A is used by Oneworld carriers <color=#3366CC>American Airlines</color>, Cathay Pacific, Malaysia Airlines and <color=#3366CC>Qantas</color>; Star
Alliance carrier Ethiopian Airlines; SkyTeam carrier XiamenAir; and non-alliance carriers including Air Austral, Air
Senegal, Air Côte d'Ivoire and <color=#3366CC>LATAM Airlines</color>.
Terminal 2B is used by Oneworld carrier Royal Air Maroc; Star Alliance carrier ITA Airways; SkyTeam carrier
Scandinavian Airlines; and non-alliance airlines including AirBaltic, Air Montenegro, El Al, JetBlue, KM Malta Airlines
and Sky Express.
Terminal 2C is used by Oneworld carriers <color=#3366CC>British Airways</color>, Oman Air and Royal Jordanian; Star Alliance carriers Air
Canada and <color=#3366CC>Air India</color>; SkyTeam carriers Aeromexico, Kenya Airways, Middle East Airlines and Vietnam Airlines; and
non-alliance carriers including Aircalin, Air Seychelles, <color=#3366CC>Emirates</color>, Gulf Air and WestJet.
Terminal 2D is used by Oneworld carrier Finnair; Star Alliance carriers Aegean Airlines, Croatia Airlines and LOT Polish
Airlines; and non-alliance carriers including Air Tahiti Nui, Air Serbia, Atlantic Airways, easyJet, Air Algérie, Georgian
Airways and Norwegian Air Shuttle.
Terminal 2E is used by <color=#3366CC>Air France</color> and its SkyTeam partners China Eastern Airlines, <color=#3366CC>Delta Air Lines</color>, <color=#3366CC>Korean Air</color> and
Middle East Airlines; Oneworld carrier Japan Airlines; and non-alliance carriers including Air Mauritius, <color=#3366CC>China Southern</color>
<color=#3366CC>Airlines</color> and Madagascar Airlines.
Terminal 2F is used by <color=#3366CC>Air France</color> and its SkyTeam partners <color=#3366CC>KLM</color> and TAROM.
Collapse of Terminal 2E
On 23 May 2004, shortly after the inauguration of terminal 2E, a portion of it collapsed near Gate E50, killing four
people. Two of the dead were reported to be Chinese citizens, one Czech and the other Lebanese.
On 17 March 2005, ADP decided to tear down and rebuild the whole part of Terminal 2E (the "jetty") of which a section
had collapsed, at a cost of approximately €100 million.
Recent terminal reassignments
Further, in April 2013, Terminal 2B closed for a complete renovation (with all airlines relocating to 2D) and received
upgrades including the addition of a second floor completely dedicated to arrivals. Terminal 2B reopened on 2 June
2021. Airlines including the <color=#3366CC>Lufthansa group</color>, Aegean Airlines, easyJet, Icelandair, LOT Polish Airlines, Norwegian Air
Shuttle, Play, Royal Air Maroc, and Scandinavian Airlines began operations at Terminal 2B until 2 December 2022,
when the airlines except easyJet and Royal Air Maroc moved back to Terminal 1. Low-cost carrier easyJet has shown
interest in being the sole carrier at 2B. To facilitate connections, a new boarding area between 2A and 2C was opened
in March 2012. It allows for all security and passport control to be handled in a single area, allows for many new
shopping opportunities as well as new airline lounges, and eases transfer restrictions between 2A and 2C. Terminal 2D
was closed during the pandemic and received the same upgrade including an additional floor. Terminal 2D reopened
on 18 April 2023 and some airlines have moved operations to the terminal.
Terminal 3
Terminal 3 is voted 2024 best low-cost airlines terminal in the world by Skytrax.
Terminal usage during COVID-19 pandemic
The airport's services during the pandemic were sharply reduced. On 30 March 2020, the airport announced it would
temporarily close Terminals 1 and 3, moving all remaining flights to Terminal 2. Terminal 2D was also closed during the
pandemic and only Terminals 2A, 2C, 2E, 2F and 2G were opened. At the beginning of the pandemic, airlines were
grouped by alliances: Star Alliance airlines operated at Terminal 2A, where Air Canada and Ethiopian Airlines operated
prior to the pandemic, Oneworld airlines shifted their operations to Terminal 2C, and SkyTeam airlines operated at
Terminals 2E and 2F. Between December 2020 and June 2021, only Terminals 2E and 2F were opened with
non-Schengen flights operating at Terminal 2E and Schengen flights operated at Terminal 2F. 2B reopened on 2 June
2021 and some airlines were shifted to that concourse. Terminals 2A, 2C and 2D were then reopened for more space.
Between June 2021 and December 2022, Star Alliance airlines operated at Terminals 2A (non-Schengen) and 2B
(Schengen), Oneworld airlines operated at Terminals 2C (non-Schengen) and 2D (Schengen) and SkyTeam airlines
operated at Terminals 2E (non-Schengen), 2F and 2G (both Schengen). However, Star Alliance airlines flights to Asia
except Singapore Airlines, who operated at Terminal 2A were operating at Terminal 2E due to the capacity restrictions
at Terminal 2A. Terminal 3 reopened on 3 May 2022 for the use of all charter and low cost airlines. Terminal 1
remained closed for renovation at that time. It reopened on 1 December 2022 to reduce traffic at Terminal 2.
Cancelled project for Terminal 4
Plans for a new terminal, Terminal 4, were first announced in 2014. With an estimated cost of €9bn, the new terminal
was to be built around 2025, when Charles de Gaulle Airport's maximum capacity of 80 million would have been
reached. When constructed, the new terminal would have been able to accommodate 30–40 million passengers per
year and would have likely been built north of Terminal 2E. However, the Terminal 4 proposal was cancelled in 2021
due to reduced traffic resulting from the <color=#3366CC>COVID-19 pandemic</color> and new environmental regulations making the project
unfeasible. Environmentalist groups hailed the cancellation of the project as a "great victory."
Roissypôle
Roissypôle is a complex consisting of office buildings, shopping areas, hotels, and a bus coach and RER B station
within Charles de Gaulle Airport. The complex includes the head office of Air France, Continental Square, the Hilton
Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport, and le Dôme building. Le Dôme includes the head office of Air France Consulting, an
Air France subsidiary. Continental Square has the head office of Air France subsidiary Servair and the Air France
Vaccinations Centre.

Ground transportation
CDGVAL
The airport's terminals are served by a free automated shuttle rail system, consisting of two lines (CDGVAL and LISA).
CDGVAL (Charles de Gaulle Véhicule Automatique Léger, English: Charles de Gaulle light automatic vehicle) links
Terminal 1, parking lot PR, Aéroport Charles de Gaulle 1 RER station (located inside Roissypôle and next to Terminal
3), Parking lot PX, and the Aéroport Charles de Gaulle 2 TGV and RER station located between Terminals 2C, 2D, 2E,
and 2F
LISA (Liaison Interne Satellite Aérogare, English: Connection internal satellite terminal) links Terminal 2E to the
Satellite S3 (L Gates) and Satellite S4 (M Gates).
RER
Charles de Gaulle Airport is connected to central Paris by the RER B, a hybrid <color=#3366CC>suburban commuter</color> and <color=#3366CC>rapid transit</color>
line. The service has two stations on the airport grounds:
• Aéroport Charles de Gaulle 1 station, located inside Roissypôle and next to Terminal 3. The station provides the
fastest access to Terminal 1 via a connection on CDGVAL.
• Aéroport Charles de Gaulle 2 TGV station, located between Terminals 2C, 2D, 2E, and 2F.
During most times, there are two types of services that operate on the RER B between Charles de Gaulle airport and
Paris:
• 4 trains per hour making all stops between Charles de Gaulle airport and Saint-Rémy-lès-Chevreuse
• 4 trains per hour that offer non-stop express service between Charles de Gaulle airport, Aulnay-sous-Bois, and
Gare du Nord, and then all stops to Massy–Palaiseau

Viktor Tsoi
Viktor Robertovich Tsoi (21 June 1962 – 15 August 1990) was a Soviet singer-songwriter and actor who co-founded
<color=#3366CC>Kino</color>, one of the most popular and influential bands in the history of <color=#3366CC>Russian music</color>.
Born and raised in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg) to a Russian mother and Koryo-saram father, Tsoi started writing
songs as a teenager. Throughout his career, Tsoi contributed a plethora of musical and artistic works, including ten
albums. After Kino appeared and performed in the 1987 Soviet film Assa, the band's popularity surged, triggering a
period referred to as "Kinomania", and leading to Tsoi's leading role in the 1988 Kazakh new wave <color=#3366CC>art film</color> The Needle.
In 1990, after a high-profile concert at Moscow’s <color=#3366CC>Luzhniki Stadium</color>, Tsoi briefly relocated to <color=#3366CC>Latvia</color> with bandmate Yuri
Kasparyan to work on the band's next album. Two months after the concert, Tsoi died in a <color=#3366CC>traffic collision</color>.
Tsoi was one of the most important pioneers of rock music in Russia and is credited with popularizing the genre
throughout the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color>. Becoming popular by combining his music and lyrics with philosophy, he retains a
devoted following throughout the <color=#3366CC>former Soviet Union</color>, where he is known as one of the most influential and popular
people in the history of <color=#3366CC>Russian music</color>.
Life and career
Early years
Viktor Robertovich Tsoi was born on 21 June 1962, in a maternity hospital on Kuznetsovskaya Street in Leningrad. He
was the only child of Valentina Vasilyevna Tsoi, a Russian schoolteacher, and Robert Maximovich Tsoi, a Soviet
Korean engineer from <color=#3366CC>Kyzylorda</color>, Kazakhstan, where his Korean parents had been exiled after Stalin's 1937
deportation of Koreans in the Soviet Union. The family's Korean ancestry can be traced back to Kimchaek (Songjin) in
the present-day <color=#3366CC>North Korea</color>, where Viktor's great-grandfather Choi Yong-nam was born in 1893.
Tsoi's Korean clan was the Wonju Choe clan, sometimes spelled as Choi. Koryo-saram, ethnic Koreans living in the
former <color=#3366CC>USSR</color>, preferred the surname Tsoi as a romanization of the <color=#3366CC>cyrillic</color>. Translated from Korean, the surname Choi
means "height" or "top".
Tsoi grew up in the vicinity of the Moskovsky Victory Park. The family lived in the notable "general's house" at the
corner of Moskovsky Avenue and Basseynaya Street. For some time, Tsoi studied at a nearby school on Frunze Street,
where his mother worked.
From 1974 until 1977, Tsoi attended a secondary art school, where he was a member of the band Palata No. 6
(Russian: No 6, English: "Ward No. 6"). The only surviving recording of the group is an album titled "Slonolunie" (a
portmanteau of slon, “elephant”, and polnolunie, “full moon”). Around the same time, he wrote his first two songs –
"Vasya Loves Disco" and "Idiot", though neither were ever performed.
From 1977, he attended the Serov Art School, until he was expelled in 1979 for poor academic performance.
Afterwards, he attended SGPTU-61, a secondary city vocational school, where he studied to become a <color=#3366CC>woodcarver</color>. In
his youth, he was a fan of Mikhail Boyarsky and <color=#3366CC>Vladimir Vysotsky</color>, and later <color=#3366CC>Bruce Lee</color>, after whom he started
modelling his image. He was fond of <color=#3366CC>martial arts</color> and often sparred "in Chinese" with bandmate Yuri Kasparyan.
First steps in music
Tsoi began writing songs at the age of 17. In the 1970s and the 1980s, <color=#3366CC>rock music</color> was an underground movement
limited mostly to Leningrad. <color=#3366CC>Moscow</color> pop stars, endorsed by the Soviet state, ruled the charts and received the most
exposure from the media. Rock music was not popular with the government, and rock bands received little to no
funding and were given little exposure by the media. The Leningrad Rock Club was one of the few public places where
rock bands were allowed to perform.
In the late 1970s and early 1980s, Tsoi was a close friend of <color=#3366CC>Alexei Rybin</color>. Rybin, a member of the hard rock band
Piligrimy, and Tsoi, who played bass guitar in the group Palata # 6 (Russian: No 6), met at the house of Andrei "Svin"
Panov, in whose apartment people and musicians often gathered, and also where his own punk band Avtomaticheskie
udovletvoriteli rehearsed. By this time, Tsoi began to perform the songs he wrote at parties.
Tsoi and Rybin, as members of (Avtomaticheskie udovletvoriteli), went to <color=#3366CC>Moscow</color> and performed <color=#3366CC>punk-rock metal</color> at
Artemy Troitsky's underground concerts. During a similar performance in Leningrad on the occasion of Andrei Tropillo's
anniversary, Tsoi and Rybin first met Boris Grebenshchikov. Later, after a solo concert by Grebenshchikov, they met up
and Tsoi played two of his songs to him. Grebenshchikov, who had already been a relatively established musician in
the Leningrad underground scene, was very impressed by Tsoi's talent and helped him start up his own band.
Beginnings of Kino
At the Leningrad Rock Club, Tsoi played as a solo artist supported by members of the band <color=#3366CC>Aquarium</color>. Tsoi's lyrics and
music impressed the crowd. In the summer of 1981, Tsoi, Rybin, and Oleg Valinsky formed the band Garin i
giperboloydy. The name was an homage to the classic Russian novel The Hyperboloid of Engineer Garin by <color=#3366CC>Aleksey</color>
<color=#3366CC>Tolstoy</color>. In autumn 1981, the band was admitted to membership of the Leningrad Rock Club. Not long after, Valinsky
was <color=#3366CC>conscripted into the army</color>, leaving only Tsoi and Rybin, who renamed the band to Kino. Kino began recording its
debut album in the spring of 1982.
First albums
In the spring of 1982, Kino began recording its debut album 45 at Andrei Tropillo's studio. Members of Aquarium took
part in the recording, with Boris Grebenshchikov directing the album. By the summer, the album was completely
finished. Its duration was 45 minutes, after which the album was named 45. The album got some distribution and Kino
performed in many apartment concerts in <color=#3366CC>Moscow</color> and Leningrad.
On 19 February 1983, a joint concert with Kino and Aquarium took place. After the concert, Yuri Kasparyan was invited
to join the band as a guitarist. In the spring, Rybin left Kino due to disagreements with Tsoi. Tsoi and Kasparyan spent
the summer on joint rehearsals. As a result, Kino recorded the album 46, which was initially thought of as a demo for
Nachalnik Kamchatki. 46 was widely distributed and was considered to be a full-fledged album. In the fall of 1983, Tsoi
went to a <color=#3366CC>psychiatric hospital</color> in Pryazhka, where he spent a month and a half. As a result, Tsoi was not conscripted
into the army. After being discharged from the psychiatric hospital, he wrote the song "Trankvilizator".
"Peremen!" ("Changes"), first performed by Tsoi in the summer of 1986, became heavily associated with the social
shifts of the <color=#3366CC>Perestroika</color> era and later saw use in various post-Soviet political movements, such as the 2020–2021
Belarusian protests.
Despite the song later becoming a staple of political demonstrations, its politicization took place against the wishes of
Viktor Tsoi, who insisted that the track was not a protest song.
Rise to fame
1987 marked a major turning point for Kino with the release of their 6th album Gruppa krovi, which sparked widespread
public devotion known as "Kinomania." Benefiting from the cultural shifts of <color=#3366CC>Glasnost</color>, the album allowed the band to
record with a polished, spacious production style and sophisticated sound that set a new standard for Soviet rock.
The album's atmospheric soundscapes and distinct lyrical themes resonated deeply with youth across the <color=#3366CC>Soviet</color>
<color=#3366CC>Union</color>, propelling Kino to mainstream prominence. Songs from the record were widely shared, and fans across the
diverse Soviet republics translated the originally <color=#3366CC>Russian</color> lyrics into their native languages as the band's cultural reach
expanded nationwide.
Over the next few years, Tsoi appeared in several successful movies and also travelled to the <color=#3366CC>United States</color> to promote
his films at <color=#3366CC>film festivals</color>. Several more albums were released, continuing to resonate deeply with listeners and further
fueling the band's massive popularity. Even though Tsoi was a huge star, he still lived a relatively ordinary life. He kept
his old job in the boiler room of an apartment building, called Kamchatka, which is currently a museum/club dedicated
to the singer.
The fact that he worked at a boiler plant surprised many people. Tsoi said that he enjoyed the work and he also needed
the money to support the band, as they still received no government support and their albums were copied and passed
around the nation via Magnitizdat free of charge. This made Tsoi even more popular among the people because it
showed that he was down to earth and they could relate to him. He also went on tour in 1988–1989 to <color=#3366CC>Italy</color>, <color=#3366CC>France</color>,
and <color=#3366CC>Denmark</color>. Kino's finest hour came in 1990 with a concert at <color=#3366CC>Moscow</color>'s <color=#3366CC>Luzhniki Stadium</color>; 62,000 fans filled the
stands to celebrate the triumph of the USSR's most successful rock group. It also was one of the four times the
<color=#3366CC>Luzhniki Olympic Fire</color> was ever lit.
Film appearances
In 1987, the band <color=#3366CC>Kino</color>, along with other Russian rock bands, appeared as themselves in Assa (<color=#3366CC>Russian</color>: ), a film by
Sergei Solovyov. The film features underground rock music prominently, with Kino making a notable concluding
performance appearance.
In 1988, Viktor Tsoi starred as the protagonist in The Needle (Russian: Igla), directed by Rashid Nugmanov and written
by Aleksandr Baranov and Bakhyt Kilibayev. The plot is centered around the character Moro, who returns to <color=#3366CC>Almaty</color>,
Kazakhstan, to collect money owed to him. While waiting out an unexpected delay, he visits his former girlfriend Dina
and discovers she has become a <color=#3366CC>morphine</color> addict. He decides to help her quit and fight the local drug mafia
responsible for her condition. But Moro finds a deadly opponent in "the doctor," the mafia kingpin who is exploiting
Dina. Tsoi was nominated for an award for his role in the film.
The film's soundtrack, including original music by Tsoi's band Kino, contributes to the overall feeling of the movie, in
addition to the film's use of post-modern twists and surreal scenes.
The film premiered in the Soviet Union in March 1988.
Death
On 15 August 1990, in Latvia, Tsoi was driving on the Sloka – Talsi highway, near Tukums and Engure. At 12:28 p.m.,
Tsoi died in a car collision. The investigation concluded that Tsoi had fallen asleep while driving, possibly due to
<color=#3366CC>fatigue</color>. He had not consumed <color=#3366CC>alcohol</color> for at least 48 hours before his death.
At the time he fell asleep, Tsoi was driving at a speed of at least 100 km/h, causing his dark blue Moskvitch-2141 to
turn into the oncoming lane and collide with an Ikarus 250 bus, 35 km on the highway from Sloka. Tsoi was pronounced
dead at the scene. Neither the driver nor the bus were badly injured or damaged. Tsoi's car was completely destroyed,
to the point that one of its tires was never found.
The death of Viktor Tsoi was a shock to many fans, with several reportedly killing themselves out of grief. On 17
August, Komsomolskaya Pravda, one of the main Soviet newspapers, had the following to say about Tsoi and his
meaning to the youth of the nation:
Tsoi means more to the young people of our nation than any politician, celebrity or writer. This is because Tsoi never
lied and never sold out. He was and remains himself. It's impossible not to believe him... Tsoi is the only rocker who
has no difference between his image and his real life, he lived the way he sang... Tsoi is the last hero of rock.
On 19 August, he was buried in a closed casket at the Bogoslovskoe Cemetery in Leningrad. Thousands of people
came to the funeral.
Kasparyan left for Leningrad prior to the collision, with a tape containing the only recording of Tsoi's vocals for the
band's next album. The remaining members of Kino finished and released the Black Album in December. It later
became one of the band's most popular albums.
Personal life
Viktor lived with his wife, Marianna Tsoi, and his son Alexander (born 1985). Tsoi lived a poor life, with Marianna saying
that they could not even afford a proper wedding dress. The apartment building boiler room he worked at was
nicknamed "<color=#3366CC>Kamchatka</color>", and is now the site of a museum and rock club dedicated to Tsoi. He also previously worked
in <color=#3366CC>Kiev</color>, Ukrainian SSR, but after the authorities found out he was working illegally, he was sent to <color=#3366CC>Moscow</color>.
During the filming of Assa, Tsoi met Natalia Razlogova, the director's assistant. Tsoi later fell in love with Razlogova
and separated from Marianna. However, they did not divorce, for the sake of their son.
Legacy
Portraits of Viktor Tsoi are displayed today in many places around Russia, from graffiti on the fences of Saint
Petersburg to an entire wall dedicated to Viktor Tsoi in a bylane of the famous Arbat Street in Moscow, where fans still
gather to remember their hero. Other Tsoi Walls can also be found in <color=#3366CC>Minsk, Belarus</color> and in some regions of
Kazakhstan. In 2000 some of the nation's top rock bands came together and released their interpretations of Kino's
best songs as a tribute to Viktor Tsoi on what would have been his 38th birthday.
In 2012, on what would have been Tsoi's 50th birthday, the remaining members of Kino gathered to record the song
"Ataman", with his vocals that were recovered from his car crash but never used because of its poor quality. The
drummer Georgiy Guryanov died in July 2013, making "Ataman" the last song recorded by Kino and its members.
On 15 August 2020, the 30th anniversary of Tsoi's death was marked. In memory of Tsoi, the Palace Bridge in St.
Petersburg was lifted to his songs. Fans across the country commemorated his death, especially in his home city of St.
Petersburg where a number of events and concerts were organised, as well as at the Tsoi Wall in <color=#3366CC>Moscow</color>. The day
before, a 4 m tall monument dedicated to Tsoi was erected in St. Petersburg in his memory.
The South Korean rock band YB covered the song "Gruppa krovi" on their 1999 album Korean Rock Remade (Korean:
ROCK ).
Viktor An, a South Korean-born Russian <color=#3366CC>short track speed skater</color>, chose his Russian name "Viktor" in honour of Tsoi.

Lisp (programming language)
Lisp (historically LISP, an abbreviation of "list processing") is a family of <color=#3366CC>programming languages</color> with a long history and
a distinctive, fully <color=#3366CC>parenthesized</color> prefix notation. Originally specified in the late 1950s, it is the second-oldest <color=#3366CC>high-level</color>
<color=#3366CC>programming language</color> still in common use, after <color=#3366CC>Fortran</color>. Lisp has changed since its early days, and many <color=#3366CC>dialects</color>
have existed over its history. Today, the best-known general-purpose Lisp dialects are Common Lisp, Scheme, Racket,
and Clojure.
Lisp was originally created as a practical <color=#3366CC>mathematical notation</color> for <color=#3366CC>computer programs</color>, influenced by (though not
originally derived from) the notation of <color=#3366CC>Alonzo Church</color>'s <color=#3366CC>lambda calculus</color>. It quickly became a favored programming
language for <color=#3366CC>artificial intelligence</color> (AI) research. As one of the earliest programming languages, Lisp pioneered many
ideas in <color=#3366CC>computer science</color>, including <color=#3366CC>tree data structures</color>, automatic storage management, dynamic typing,
conditionals, higher-order functions, <color=#3366CC>recursion</color>, the self-hosting compiler, and the read–eval–print loop.
The name LISP derives from "List Processor". <color=#3366CC>Linked lists</color> are one of Lisp's major <color=#3366CC>data structures</color>, and Lisp <color=#3366CC>source</color>
<color=#3366CC>code</color> is made of lists. Thus, Lisp programs can manipulate source code as a data structure, giving rise to the <color=#3366CC>macro</color>
systems that allow programmers to create new syntax or new domain-specific languages embedded in Lisp.
The interchangeability of code and data gives Lisp its instantly recognizable syntax. All program code is written as
s-expressions, or parenthesized lists. A function call or syntactic form is written as a list with the function or operator's
name first, and the arguments following; for instance, a function that takes three arguments would be called as.
History
<color=#3366CC>John McCarthy</color> began developing Lisp in 1958 while he was at the <color=#3366CC>Massachusetts Institute of Technology</color> (MIT). He
was motivated by a desire to create an <color=#3366CC>artificial intelligence</color> (AI) programming language that would work on the IBM
704, as he believed that "IBM looked like a good bet to pursue Artificial Intelligence research vigorously." He was
inspired by Information Processing Language, which was also based on list processing, but did not use it because it
was designed for different hardware and he found an algebraic language more appealing. Due to these factors, he
consulted on the design of the <color=#3366CC>Fortran</color> List Processing Language, which was implemented as a Fortran library.
However, he was dissatisfied with it because it did not support <color=#3366CC>recursion</color> or a modern if-then-else statement (which was
a new concept when Lisp was first introduced).
McCarthy's original notation used bracketed "M-expressions" that would be translated into S-expressions. As an
example, the M-expression is equivalent to the S-expression. Once Lisp was implemented, programmers rapidly chose
to use S-expressions, and M-expressions were abandoned. M-expressions surfaced again with short-lived attempts of
MLisp by Horace Enea and CGOL by Vaughan Pratt.
Lisp was first implemented by Steve Russell on an IBM 704 computer using <color=#3366CC>punched cards</color>. Russell was working for
McCarthy at the time and realized (to McCarthy's surprise) that the Lisp eval function could be implemented in <color=#3366CC>machine</color>
<color=#3366CC>code</color>.
According to McCarthy
Steve Russell said, look, why don't I program this eval ... and I said to him, boss, boss, you're confusing theory with
practice, this eval is intended for reading, not for computing. But he went ahead and did it. That is, he <color=#3366CC>compiled</color> the eval
in my paper into IBM 704 machine code, fixing <color=#3366CC>bugs</color>, and then advertised this as a Lisp interpreter, which it certainly
was. So at that point Lisp had essentially the form that it has today ...
The result was a working Lisp <color=#3366CC>interpreter</color> which could be used to run Lisp programs, or more properly, "evaluate Lisp
expressions".
Two <color=#3366CC>assembly language macros</color> for the IBM 704 became the primitive operations for decomposing lists: car (Contents
of the Address part of Register number) and cdr (Contents of the Decrement part of Register number), where "register"
refers to <color=#3366CC>registers</color> of the computer's <color=#3366CC>central processing unit</color> (CPU). Lisp dialects still use and for the operations that
return the first item in a list and the rest of the list, respectively.
McCarthy published Lisp's design in a paper in Communications of the ACM on April 1, 1960, entitled "Recursive
Functions of Symbolic Expressions and Their Computation by Machine, Part I". He showed that with a few simple
operators and a notation for anonymous functions borrowed from Church, one can build a Turing-complete language
for algorithms.
The first complete Lisp compiler, written in Lisp, was implemented in 1962 by Tim Hart and Mike Levin at MIT, and
could be compiled by simply having an existing LISP interpreter interpret the compiler code, producing <color=#3366CC>machine code</color>
output able to be executed at a 40-fold improvement in speed over that of the interpreter. This compiler introduced the
Lisp model of incremental compilation, in which compiled and interpreted functions can intermix freely. The language
used in Hart and Levin's memo is much closer to modern Lisp style than McCarthy's earlier code.
Garbage collection routines were developed by MIT graduate student Daniel Edwards, prior to 1962.
During the 1980s and 1990s, a great effort was made to unify the work on new Lisp dialects (mostly successors to
Maclisp such as ZetaLisp and NIL (New Implementation of Lisp)) into a single language. The new language, Common
Lisp, was somewhat compatible with the dialects it replaced (the book Common Lisp the Language notes the
compatibility of various constructs). In 1994, ANSI published the Common Lisp standard, "ANSI X3.226-1994
Information Technology Programming Language Common Lisp".
Timeline
Connection to artificial intelligence
Since its inception, Lisp was closely connected with the AI research community, especially on PDP-10 systems. Lisp
was used as the implementation of the language Micro Planner, which was used in the famous AI system SHRDLU. In
the 1970s, as AI research spawned commercial offshoots, the performance of existing Lisp systems became a growing
issue, as programmers needed to be familiar with the performance ramifications of the various techniques and choices
involved in the implementation of Lisp.
Genealogy and variants
Over its sixty-year history, Lisp has spawned many variations on the core theme of an S-expression language. Some of
these variations have been standardized and implemented by different groups with different priorities (for example, both
Common Lisp and Scheme have multiple implementations). However, in other cases a software project defines a Lisp
without a standard and there is no clear distinction between the dialect and the implementation (for example, Clojure
and Emacs Lisp fall into this category).
Differences between dialects (and/or implementations) may be quite visible—for instance, Common Lisp uses the
keyword defun to name a function, but Scheme uses define. Within a dialect that is standardized conforming
implementations support the same core language, but with different extensions and libraries. This sometimes also
creates quite visible changes from the base language - for instance, Guile (an implementation of Scheme) uses define*
to create functions which can have default arguments and/or keyword arguments, neither of which are standardized.
Historically significant dialects
• LISP 1 – First implementation.
• LISP 1.5 – First widely distributed version, developed by McCarthy and others at MIT. So named because it
contained several improvements on the original "LISP 1" interpreter, but was not a major restructuring as the
planned LISP 2 would be.
• Stanford LISP 1.6 – A successor to LISP 1.5 developed at the Stanford AI Lab, and widely distributed to PDP-10
systems running the TOPS-10 operating system. It was rendered obsolete by Maclisp and InterLisp.
• Maclisp – developed for MIT's Project MAC, MACLISP is a direct descendant of LISP 1.5. It ran on the PDP-10 and
Multics systems. MACLISP would later come to be called Maclisp, and is often referred to as MacLisp. The "MAC"
in MACLISP is unrelated to Apple's <color=#3366CC>Macintosh</color> or <color=#3366CC>McCarthy</color>.
• Interlisp – developed at BBN Technologies for PDP-10 systems running the TENEX operating system, later
adopted as a "West coast" Lisp for the Xerox Lisp machines as InterLisp-D. A small version called "InterLISP 65"
was published for the MOS Technology 6502-based Atari 8-bit computers. Maclisp and InterLisp were strong
competitors.
• Franz Lisp – originally a <color=#3366CC>University of California, Berkeley</color> project; later developed by Franz Inc. The name is a
humorous deformation of the name "<color=#3366CC>Franz Liszt</color>", and does not refer to Allegro Common Lisp, the dialect of
Common Lisp sold by Franz Inc., in more recent years.
• <color=#3366CC>muLISP</color> – initially developed by Albert D. Rich and David Stoutemeyer for small microcomputer systems.
Commercially available in 1979, it was running on CP/M systems of only 64KB RAM and was later ported to
MS-DOS. Development of the MS-DOS version ended in 1995. The mathematical Software "Derive" was written in
muLISP for MS-DOS and later for Windows up to 2007.
• XLISP, which AutoLISP was based on.
• Standard Lisp and Portable Standard Lisp were widely used and ported, especially with the Computer Algebra
System REDUCE.
• ZetaLisp, also termed Lisp Machine Lisp – used on the Lisp machines, direct descendant of Maclisp. ZetaLisp had
a big influence on Common Lisp.
• LeLisp is a French Lisp dialect. One of the first Interface Builders (called SOS Interface) was written in LeLisp.
• Scheme (1975).
• Common Lisp (1984), as described by Common Lisp the Language – a consolidation of several divergent attempts
(ZetaLisp, Spice Lisp, NIL, and S-1 Lisp) to create successor dialects to Maclisp, with substantive influences from
the Scheme dialect as well. This version of Common Lisp was available for wide-ranging platforms and was
accepted by many as a de facto standard until the publication of ANSI Common Lisp (ANSI X3.226-1994). Among
the most widespread sub-dialects of Common Lisp are Steel Bank Common Lisp (SBCL), CMU Common Lisp
(CMU-CL), Clozure OpenMCL (not to be confused with Clojure!), GNU CLisp, and later versions of Franz Lisp; all
of them adhere to the later ANSI CL standard (see below).

• EuLisp – attempt to develop a new efficient and cleaned-up Lisp.
• ISLISP – attempt to develop a new efficient and cleaned-up Lisp. Standardized as ISO/IEC 13816:1997 and later
revised as ISO/IEC 13816:2007: Information technology – Programming languages, their environments and system
software interfaces – Programming language ISLISP.
• IEEE Scheme – IEEE standard, 1178–1990 (R1995).
• ANSI Common Lisp – an American National Standards Institute (ANSI) <color=#3366CC>standard</color> for Common Lisp, created by

Common Lisp implementations. Although formally an ANSI standard, the implementation, sale, use, and influence

• Clojure, a recent dialect of Lisp which compiles to the <color=#3366CC>Java virtual machine</color> and has a particular focus on

• Game Oriented Assembly Lisp (or GOAL) is a video game programming language developed by Andy Gavin at
Naughty Dog. It was written using Allegro Common Lisp and used in the development of the entire Jak and Daxter
